analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to unionize and raises penalties on employers who interfere.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 224-194 on February 6, 2020, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it easier for workers to form unions and harder for employers to stop them: fines of up to $50,000 per violation (double for repeat offenders), a ban on forcing workers to attend anti-union meetings, protections against being mislabeled an independent contractor, the right to join class-action lawsuits despite arbitration clauses, and the power to override state right-to-work laws. It passed the House mostly along party lines but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize would gain the most: employers could no longer permanently replace strikers, force workers into anti-union meetings, or require them to waive their right to sue as a class, and firing a worker for organizing would trigger double damages plus fines of up to $50,000 per violation ($100,000 for repeat violations) and a private right to sue in court [S4][S5]. Workers misclassified as independent contractors would get employee status under a stricter test [S5][S2]. Unions would gain new members and could charge fees to all workers they represent, even in right-to-work states [S4][S5]. Workers forming a first union contract could turn to binding arbitration if bargaining stalls [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Firing or seriously harming a worker for organizing would cost the employer back pay, front pay, double liquidated damages, and civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat violations — current law's penalties are tiny, so violating workers' rights is often cheaper than obeying the law.

Workers could no longer be required to attend employer meetings designed to discourage union membership, and employers could be sued directly in court by workers they retaliated against, instead of waiting years for the National Labor Relations Board.
Employers could not force workers to sign away their right to join class or collective lawsuits as a condition of employment, closing a loophole created by forced-arbitration agreements.

A stricter definition of 'employee' and a broader joint-employer standard would extend labor-law protections to workers currently labeled independent contractors, and to workers whose conditions are effectively controlled by a parent company or client firm.

Once a majority of workers voted for a union, the employer would be legally required to bargain, and if no first contract were reached after mediation, a three-member arbitration panel would impose a binding two-year contract — ending the common tactic of stalling indefinitely.

Employers could not participate in the NLRB union-election proceedings and would have to hand over worker contact lists to the union, speeding up elections and limiting employer interference; collective bargaining agreements could require all represented employees to pay fees despite state right-to-work laws.

Strikers could not be permanently replaced, secondary strikes would be permitted, and consultants hired to persuade employees against unionizing would lose their reporting exemption unless they were providing true legal representation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing union drives would bear the cost: fines up to $50,000 per violation ($100,000 for repeat violations), double damages, direct lawsuits from workers, mandatory first-contract arbitration, disclosure of anti-union consulting, and loss of the ability to run captive-audience campaigns or participate in union-election proceedings [S4][S5]. The union-avoidance consulting industry would lose business as persuader arrangements lose their reporting exemption [S4]. Some costs would likely be passed to consumers through prices, and employers in right-to-work states argue the fee provisions raise their labor costs [S5].

drawbacks.text: If bargaining for a first contract stalls, a government-facilitated arbitration panel — one member picked by the union, one by the employer, one neutral — would impose a binding two-year contract based on statutory factors, taking final wage and benefits decisions out of both sides' hands.

The bill overrides state right-to-work laws, letting union contracts require all represented employees to pay fees as a condition of employment — a direct reversal of the policy choice in roughly half the states.

The new three-part test would classify many independent contractors as employees, which protects them under labor law but would take away the self-employment status and flexibility some contractors deliberately chose.

Legalizing secondary strikes would allow unions to pressure neutral companies that do business with the employer in dispute, potentially dragging uninvolved businesses into labor conflicts; the bill also repeals employers' right to sue unions over such strikes.

Employers would have no standing to participate in NLRB union-representation proceedings at all — the board would also be allowed to certify a union without a rerun election if the employer interfered with the first one — which critics said denies employers any voice in elections affecting their workplace.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill addresses a real imbalance: federal penalties for illegally firing union supporters are among the weakest in any area of employment law, and the enforcement-only remedy means many workers never get made whole. Bigger fines, double damages, and a private right to sue are straightforward deterrence. The more aggressive provisions — binding arbitration of first contracts, overriding state right-to-work laws, secondary strikes, and barring employers from election proceedings — go well beyond penalty fixes and were the main grounds for opposition, including from the 7 House Democrats who voted no. An honest supporter would concede the bill was written to shift bargaining power decisively toward unions, not just to stop illegal behavior.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House by a mostly party-line vote but was sent to a Senate committee that never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on May 2, 2019, and it drew 218 cosponsors — 216 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The House Education and Labor Committee approved it on September 25, 2019, by a vote of 26-21, and reported it in December 2019.

After a day of amendment debate, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit 195-223 and passed the bill 224-194 on February 6, 2020, with 219 Democrats in favor, 7 Democrats opposed, and only 5 of 191 Republicans in favor.

The Senate received the bill on February 10, 2020, and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and industries that spend heavily to resist unionization — including gig platforms, staffing and franchise businesses, and anti-union consultants — kept the legal status quo intact because the Senate never acted. Workers who might have organized under the new protections gained nothing from the bill's passage.

for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee; bill sponsor

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 224-194 with 219 of 226 voting Democrats in favor and 186 of 191 voting Republicans opposed; only 5 Republicans and 7 Democrats crossed lines.

industries.industry: Employers facing union drives (large service, retail, and manufacturing employers)
industries.note: The bill raised the price of firing or intimidating union supporters from near-zero to $50,000 per violation plus double damages and direct lawsuits, and took away campaign tools like captive-audience meetings and employer participation in election proceedings.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consulting and persuader law firms
industries.note: The bill stripped the reporting exemption for consultants who plan anti-union meetings, train supervisors, or target employees, shrinking a paid industry built on defeating organizing drives.
The new three-part test would make many contractors employees covered by labor law, threatening business models built on classifying workers as independent contractors.
The broadened joint-employer standard would hold franchisors and parent companies responsible for labor conditions at franchisees and client firms they control directly or indirectly.
Unions would gain members through faster elections, mandatory bargaining, first-contract arbitration, and the ability to collect fees from all represented workers even in right-to-work states.
Federal law would override the roughly half of states that ban mandatory union fees, allowing contracts to require all represented employees to pay.
